item.title: Frequency Estimation from the Internal State of the Boyer-Moore Majority Vote Algorithm
item.description: arXiv:2611.33206v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Boyer-Moore Majority Vote algorithm identifies a majority candidate in a single pass over a data stream using constant memory O(1) and linear processing time O(n). While the classic algorithm identifies a candidate without directly estimating its frequency, its internal register states retain information about item occurrences during execution. This work investigates a frequency estimator derived directly from these internal counters. We establish the conditions under which the counter state enables exact recovery of the frequency of the majority element and characterize the estimation error when these conditions are not satisfied. In particular, we analyze the effect of stream ordering on the estimator and identify delayed-arrival configurations, such as Majority-Delayed sequences, that can lead to systematic estimation errors. We further derive the error behavior associated with late-arriving majority blocks and empirically evaluate the estimator across multiple stream topologies. The results demonstrate that the internal state of the Boyer-Moore algorithm can provide frequency information without increasing its O(1) space complexity. At the same time, its accuracy depends critically on the ordering of elements in the input stream.
item.dc:creator: Saeed Momeni, Mohsen Hooshmand

item.title: Feedback Rounds and Query Costs in Sparse Product Pure Exploration
item.description: arXiv:2611.33245v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How much can one more round of feedback save when a measurement combines several settings into a single noisy reading? We study a product decision with $K$ blocks and $m$ nonbaseline labels per block. At most $s$ blocks have nonzero effects, of arbitrary sign. Each query tests labels in at most $b$ blocks. The final assignment must have total loss at most $\varepsilon$ with probability at least $1-\delta$. On the benchmark $K=s^2$, $1\le b\le s$ and $s^\nu\le m\le s^\zeta$ for fixed $0<\nu\le1\le\zeta$, we characterize two minimax costs for sufficiently large $s$. The optimal orders are $(Km/b)\chi U_B$ readings and $Km\chi U_B$ settings for $B\ge1$ batches, where $\chi=\sigma^2s^2/\varepsilon^2\ge1$ for noise proxy $\sigma^2$ and $\delta\le1/16$. The factor $U_B$ is obtained by applying $B-1$ logarithms to $\log(es)$, clipping each iterate at one and imposing a floor of $\log(1/\delta)/s$. One algorithm attains both bounds. For general dimensions, a polynomial-time algorithm attains the optimal setting cost. When $K=s^2$, $m=b=s$ and $\log(1/\delta)=s$, both fully adaptive orders are attainable in polynomial real-arithmetic time when $\chi=\Omega((s/\log(es))^{1/3})$. With identical budgets and decoder, four batches succeeded on 1,070 of 1,200 paired simulated instances and two batches on 779.
item.dc:creator: Yujiao Peng, Qifan Yang

item.title: Improved Exact Algorithms and Parameterized Results for Monopolar Graph Problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.33362v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A monopolar graph is a graph whose vertex set can be partitioned into a cluster graph and an independent set. Deciding whether such a partition exists is Monopolar Recognition. We also study three related problems: Monopolar Extension, where a partial assignment of vertices to the two sides is given and must be extended to a full monopolar partition; List Monopolar Partition, where each vertex comes with a list of allowed sides; and Monopolar Vertex Deletion, which asks for a minimum-weight vertex set whose removal makes the graph monopolar. All four problems are NP-hard, which motivates the study of faster exact algorithms for these problems. We design a new exact branching algorithm for Monopolar Extension running in O*(1.29803^n) time, improving upon the previously best-known O*(1.3734^n)-time algorithm of Philip and Sridhara [WG 2025]. The O*(.) notation suppresses factors that are bounded by a polynomial in the input size. The same bound applies to List Monopolar Partition, which is an equivalent formulation, and to Monopolar Recognition, which is a special case. It also gives an O*(2.29803^n)-time algorithm for Monopolar Vertex Deletion. We further present the first explicit fixed-parameter algorithms with concrete single-exponential dependence on treewidth for these problems. We show that Monopolar Extension, and hence also List Monopolar Partition and Monopolar Recognition, can be solved in 3^tw*n^O(1) time. For Monopolar Vertex Deletion we obtain a running time of 5^tw*n^O(1), which improves to 4^tw*n^O(1) when the weights are integers bounded by a polynomial in n.
item.dc:creator: Soumen Mandal, Ashutosh Rai

item.title: Fast Algorithms for Permanents of Permutationally-Dominant Matrices
item.description: arXiv:2611.33485v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a fast algorithm for approximating the permanent of permutationally-dominant matrices. In particular, we obtain a fully polynomial randomised approximation scheme whose runtime is quadratic in both the dimension of the matrix and the inverse of the approximation error. Our approach is based on a polymer model representation of the permanent and importance sampling of the logarithm of its partition function via the theory of heaps of pieces of Viennot.
item.dc:creator: Ryan L. Mann

item.title: Online Network Design with Batch Processing
item.description: arXiv:2611.33678v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: An online service chooses which waiting jobs to start together. Each finishes after its own processing time, and the longest determines the next possible launch. We charge network cost plus either total flow or the sum of per-batch maximum flows. For TCP acknowledgment with a fixed fee per launch, the optimal deterministic total-flow ratio is \(1+\rho\), where \(\rho\) is the processing-time spread. For batch maxima, a union of intervals on the release-time axis gives the exact offline cost when batches may overlap. It yields an offline \(2\)-approximation and pays for an online timer of ratio five. The optimal deterministic ratio is two at equal lengths and lies in \([2+2\sqrt2,5]\) at unrestricted spread. How often can later batches incur the same blocking delay? Rooted purchases can be combined, giving a polynomial-time \(3+2\sqrt2\) guarantee for batch maxima on undirected Steiner networks. A mobile server can concatenate walks in order, transferring an instantaneous maximum-wait ratio \(\alpha\) to a batch-maximum flow ratio \(3\alpha+6\). With \(k\) ephemeral facilities sharing one processor and one site per launch, separate openings can each incur the wait. The optimal deterministic batch-maximum ratio is then \(\Theta(k)\) at unrestricted spread. The upper bound uses exact assignments, computable in polynomial time for fixed \(k\).
item.dc:creator: Tianhang Lu, Runtian Ren, Shengcai Liu

item.title: SAT-Driven Exact Treewidth via Safe Separators and Structure-Aware Encodings
item.description: arXiv:2611.33695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Treewidth is a standard measure of graph structure, but computing it exactly is NP-hard. SAT- and MaxSAT-based approaches provide a uniform way to solve treewidth by encoding it in conjunctive normal form and delegating the search to modern Boolean solvers, thus directly benefiting from continued progress in SAT technology. This report studies how to strengthen such SAT-driven solvers with structural reasoning and low-overhead guidance, both at the meta-algorithmic level and within the encoding itself. Starting from a baseline SAT/MaxSAT formulation, we investigate structure-based simplifications that reduce solver effort while preserving exactness, and we evaluate practical heuristic enhancements (fast upper/lower bounds and solver guidance) within iterative SAT and MaxSAT workflows. Experiments show consistent speedups on instances with exploitable structure, and clarify where SAT-based approaches remain limited.
item.dc:creator: Yannik Krone

item.title: Toggle Tree: A New Data Structure for Efficient Parallel Graph Processing
item.description: arXiv:2611.33738v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present the Toggle Tree, a parallel data structure for frontier-based graph algorithms. A Toggle Tree is used to represent a subset of vertices using hierarchical bit vectors, enabling efficient parallel updates, traversal, and set-wise reductions without global packing. It provides an IndexSet interface that unifies a wide range of parallel graph algorithms under a common abstraction of frontiers and active sets, and an IndexMap interface that also incorporates priority-queue semantics. Specifically, the Toggle Tree aims to combine the advantages of traditional sparse and dense frontier representations, offering both provable theoretical guarantees and high efficiency in practice. Using Toggle Trees, we implement five fundamental graph algorithms, including breadth-first search (BFS), k-core, degree-based graph coloring, single-source shortest paths using Bellman-Ford, and weighted-BFS (wBFS). Across a diverse set of large real-world graphs and the five graph problems, our implementations outperform state-of-the-art baselines, including GBBS and PASGAL, achieving substantial speedups. Our code is publicly available.
item.dc:creator: Xinjian Jiang, Youzhe Liu, Yan Gu, Yihan Sun

item.title: A Polynomial-Time Algorithm for ARRIVAL
item.description: arXiv:2611.33785v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In ARRIVAL, a token moves through a directed graph from a specified starting vertex, alternating between the two outgoing arcs of each vertex on successive departures. The problem asks whether the token ever reaches a given destination. Although the walk can be exponentially long, we give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm, resolving an open problem. We first average the local routing rules and then restore the original rules on selected periods. The number of refinement rounds is at most the number of nonterminal vertices. The algorithm extends to explicitly given cyclic successor lists. It also computes exact departure counts when every nonterminal vertex has a path to an absorbing terminal and recovers the configuration of the walk at any binary-encoded time.
item.dc:creator: Chenglin Fan, Jeonseong Kim

item.title: Almost Tight Hardness of Approximation for $0$-Extension
item.description: arXiv:2611.33928v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In the $0$-Extension problem, we are given an undirected graph $G=(V,E)$ with non-negative edge weights $w: E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$, a collection $T \subseteq V$ of $k$ terminals, and a metric $D$ over terminals $T$. The goal is to find a retraction $f:V\rightarrow T$ that maps every terminal to itself, while minimizing the sum over all edges of the product of the edge's weight and the distance in $D$ between the terminals to which its endpoints are assigned, i.e., \[ \sum_{\{u,v\}\in E} w_{\{u,v\}} \cdot D(f(u), f(v)). \] Fakcharoenphol, Harrelson, Rao, and Talwar achieve the best known approximation ratio of $O(\log k / \log \log k)$, while the known approximation hardness is $\Omega(\sqrt{\log k})$ assuming the unique games conjecture. In this work, we establish an $\Omega(\log^{1-\varepsilon}k)$ hardness of approximation for every constant $\varepsilon\in (0,1)$ and arbitrarily large fixed $k$, almost matching the upper bound in the exponent of $\log k$. The main technical contribution is an $\Omega(\log^{1-\varepsilon}k)$ integrality gap for the earthmover relaxation. Our construction is inspired by randomized extensions of expanders introduced by Schwartz and Tur for the metric relaxation. The result then follows from an existing theorem by Manokaran, Naor, Raghavendra, and Schwartz that translates the integrality gap for the earthmover relaxation to the approximation hardness for every fixed $k$.
item.dc:creator: Qingyun Chen, Weihao Zhu

item.title: Directed $k$-Disjoint Shortest Paths in Polynomial Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.34013v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The $k$-Disjoint Shortest Paths problem asks for pairwise vertex-disjoint shortest paths connecting $k$ prescribed terminal pairs in a graph with positive edge weights. Eilam-Tzoreff [DAM 1998] asked whether it is polynomial-time solvable for every fixed $k$. Lochet [SODA 2021] answered this for undirected graphs, while for directed graphs it has remained open for every $k\ge3$. We give a polynomial-time algorithm for directed graphs and every fixed $k$, resolving this open problem for all graphs.
item.dc:creator: Yang Cao, Haoran Qi, Hanzhi Wang

item.title: Near-Tight Robust Coresets for Clustering in Euclidean Spaces
item.description: arXiv:2611.34063v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper considers coresets for the robust $(k,z)$-clustering problem with $m$ outliers in Euclidean spaces. A robust coreset is a weighted subset of the data that, for every set of $k$ centers and every outlier budget $0\leq b\leq m$, approximates the clustering cost with $b$ outliers removed to within relative error $\epsilon$. For every constant $z\geq 1$, we prove that the optimal worst-case size of such coresets over all ambient dimensions is \[ \Theta(m) + \widetilde{\Theta}_z(\min\{k\epsilon^{-(z+2)}, k^{2(z+1)/(z+2)}\epsilon^{-2} + km^{z/(z+2)}\epsilon^{-4/(z+2)}\}), \qquad 1\leq z \leq 2, \] \[ \Theta(m) + \widetilde{\Theta}_z(\min\{k\epsilon^{-(z+2)}, k^{2(z+1)/(z+2)}\epsilon^{-2} + k \min\{m, \sqrt{m}\epsilon^{-z/2}\} \}), \qquad z > 2. \]
item.dc:creator: Pengsen Huang, Yi Li, Xuan Wu

item.title: Concavity of cardinality-constrained interval stabbing and interval cover problems
item.description: arXiv:2611.34089v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the cardinality-constrained interval stabbing problem, in which the goal is to maximize the total weight of intervals hit by at least one of at most $k$ selected points. Although this problem does not admit a simple greedy solution, we show that its optimal value is a concave function of $k$. We establish this result using a linear programming formulation whose relaxation always admits an optimal solution with integer values. This allows us to prove concavity for the original problem. We further extend the result to the related interval cover problem. These concavity properties provide a basis for applying Lagrangian optimization using algorithms for the corresponding unconstrained problems.
item.dc:creator: Janez Brank, Toma\v{z} Ho\v{c}evar

item.title: Parameterized Algorithms for Minimum Sum Vertex Cover on Dense Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.34312v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The \textsc{Minimum Sum Vertex Cover} (MSVC) problem asks for a linear ordering of the vertices of a graph that minimizes the sum, over all edges, of the position of the earlier endpoint. We study its parameterized complexity on graphs that become a clique, cluster graph, or a split graph after deleting a small set of vertices, called the Modulator. We prove that MSVC is fixed-parameter tractable when parameterized jointly by the cluster modulator size and the maximum clique size in the remaining cluster graph, while allowing arbitrarily many cliques. For the clique modulator parameterization, we present a combinatorial algorithm that avoids the integer quadratic programming used in prior work [Aute, Panolan, Theoretical Computer Science, 2025]. We also introduce a vertex-weighted formulation of MSVC and obtain an XP algorithm parameterized by the clique modulator size. Using this algorithm as a subroutine, we develop an XP algorithm parameterized by the split modulator size. These results extend the known structural parameterizations of MSVC and highlight weighted MSVC as a promising direction for further research.
item.dc:creator: Shubhada Aute, Noleen K\"ohler, Fahad Panolan

item.title: Uniform Guarded Bootstrapping for Topology-Sensitive Directed Shortest Paths
item.description: arXiv:2611.34600v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: On a source star, every leaf distance is an input weight. Thus computing labeled distances need not reveal their order. For a rooted directed topology, let $K$ be the least worst-case sum of comparisons and additions among finite deterministic programs specialized to that topology and correct for every nonnegative weighting. We give one deterministic program that takes the graph as input. This graph-input-uniform algorithm has total comparison-addition RAM time $O(m+n+K\Phi(K)\exp(O(\log_2^*(K+2))))$, where $n$ and $m$ count vertices and arcs, and $\Phi$ is a regularized product of successive logarithms. An active core is the small graph remaining after directly recoverable distances are separated. The algorithm chooses its parameters from the core size. Frozen entry ceilings let each interrupted local call be replayed on a small completion, whose complete-run bound controls the stopped work. The cost coefficient satisfies a linear one-step recurrence, yielding at most exponential growth in the number of generations. This permits a depth chosen from the measured core size. For $m=O(n)$, the solver gives $O(n\sqrt{\log n}(\log\log n)^{1/4+o(1)})$ time, improving the sparse directed bound of Duan, Mao, Shu, and Yin. A complementary result uses reusable dominator calibration for changing seed vectors on a fixed weighted graph.
item.dc:creator: Bin Cai

item.title: Min-Plus Products and Dynamic Programming with Few Violations of the Adjacent Monge Inequalities
item.description: arXiv:2611.34733v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Local rewards can introduce negative adjacent mixed differences into a convex transition cost. If a cost array $B$ has $s(B)$ such differences, we express it as a Monge array minus $s(B)$ weighted rectangles and sweep its columns, maintaining the lower envelope of the active rows. For explicit finite $n\times n$ matrices $A,B$ and $L=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil$, we compute $A\otimes B$ and the smallest minimizing index for every entry in $\mathcal{O}(n^2L+ns(B)L^3)$ time and $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ space, giving near-quadratic time for arbitrary $A$ when $s(B)=\mathcal{O}(n)$, including right factors with $\Theta(n^2)$ positive differences. For block costs given by a constant-time Monge oracle and $r$ signed rectangle corrections, the sweep activates each row when its prefix optimum becomes available and computes an optimal contiguous partition in $\mathcal{O}((n+r)L^3)$ time and $\mathcal{O}(n+r)$ working space. The sweep handles convex transitions with interval rules and assigns one rectangle to each internal edge or hyperedge reward in a convex block cost, giving near-linear exact algorithms on sparse inputs for ordered graph modularity, weighted contiguous cluster editing, all-or-nothing HyperLam, and bounded-rank strict hypergraph modularity. Let $c_{\mathrm{APSP}}$ denote the deterministic exponent of all-pairs shortest paths with polynomially bounded integer weights. For fixed $3-c_{\mathrm{APSP}}<\alpha\le1$, any deterministic $\mathcal{O}(n^\beta)$-time min-plus product algorithm for polynomially bounded integer matrices with $s(B)\le n^{1+\alpha}$ satisfies $\beta\ge c_{\mathrm{APSP}}-1+\alpha$. The reduction from general integer min-plus multiplication uses right factors obtained from $(j-k)^2$ by at most $n^{1+\alpha}$ interval discounts, with $\Theta(n^2)$ positive differences and all remaining differences negative.
item.dc:creator: Yanqiao Chen

item.title: Pinwheel Scheduling is PSPACE-Complete
item.description: arXiv:2611.34869v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Pinwheel Scheduling is a classical periodic scheduling problem, receiving as input the deadlines $d_i$ of $n$ tasks and asking for an infinite schedule with one task per time unit, such that every task $i$ is scheduled at least once in every $d_i$ time units. Holte, Mok, Rosier, Tulchinsky, and Varvel introduced the problem in 1989 and showed that it lies in \(\PSPACE\). Its exact complexity has been open since then. \(\NP\)-hardness for explicitly listed deadlines was established only recently, and membership in \(\NP\) is open. In this work we prove that Pinwheel Scheduling is \(\PSPACE\)-complete when the deadlines are written in binary. This finally settles the long-standing open question about the complexity of Pinwheel Scheduling. We present a chain of reductions, starting from Periodic 3-SAT, a classical \(\PSPACE\)-complete problem, and using two newly-defined intermediate periodic scheduling problems. These intermediate problems can be seen as periodically assigning tasks to days, with each day containing a fixed number of slots (\emph{hours}) in which tasks are scheduled. In the first of these problems, each day is additionally allowed to contain \emph{breaks}, that is, hours in which no task can be scheduled.
item.dc:creator: Dimitris Fotakis, Sotiris Kanellopoulos, Giorgos Mitropoulos, Aris Pagourtzis, Christos Papadimitriou, Christos Pergaminelis, Thanos Tolias

item.title: Robust large-scale approximate solutions of the constrained Kemeny aggregation ranking problem
item.description: arXiv:2611.34873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Kemeny aggregation ranking problem consists of computing the consensus rankings of an election with respect to the well-known Kemeny-Young voting method. These consensus rankings satisfy many fundamental properties and are the geometric medians of the votes in the election under the Kendall-tau distance which counts the number of pairwise disagreements. While having various applications in computational social choice, machine learning, operations research, and biology, the problem of computing the consensus rankings is NP-hard and encounters a severe bottleneck in practice. In this paper, we consider the more general Kemeny aggregation ranking problem under immutable input pairwise constraints and propose robust and scalable approximate methods with provable guarantees. We thus provide an algorithmic solution to the more general constrained problem of incorporating a posteriori immutable pairwise constraints into past rankings (e.g., historical voter ballots or legacy laboratory assays) without incurring the cost of generating new data. Our base algorithm $\Gamma$-XCC provides a source of rankings with a bounded constant approximation factor. $\Gamma$-XCC generalizes the Copeland ranking method and satisfies the constrained Condorcet consistency property, an extension of the Condorcet winner criterion for elections with immutable pairwise constraints. Thereby, our methods provide large-scale solutions that address the reliability and explainability issues. Our algorithms are also applicable to weighted tournaments with input pairwise constraints and satisfy similar properties in this larger context.
item.dc:creator: Xuan Kien Phung, Sylvie Hamel

item.title: Linear Single-Source Shortest Path, Almost
item.description: arXiv:2611.34911v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a comparison-addition algorithm for single-source shortest paths in undirected graphs with nonnegative real edge lengths. For each input with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, its expected running time is $O(m+n\log\log\log n)$. It terminates almost surely. Every terminating run returns exact distances and a shortest-path tree on the reachable vertices. The bound is independent of the ratio of edge lengths and is linear whenever $m=\Omega(n\log\log\log n)$.
item.dc:creator: Iman Gholami, MohammadTaghi Hajiaghayi

item.title: PAC Learning to Sample: On Computational Aspects of Language Generation
item.description: arXiv:2611.33464v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The success of language models has motivated theoretical work on learning to sample from distributions on discrete domains. A prominent abstraction is the model of language generation in the limit, introduced by Kleinberg and Mullainathan (NeurIPS 2024), in which the algorithm must generate from the target language after some finite but unspecified number of positive examples. While its positive results are surprisingly general, most guarantees are qualitative. In this work, we seek quantitative guarantees on sample and time complexity, inspired by statistical and computational learning theory. To this end, we study a PAC model of language generation, proposed (in a different context) by De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio (SODA 2015), in which a Boolean concept class $C$ over $\{-1,1\}^n$ defines the target languages: given uniformly random positive examples of an unknown concept $f \in C$, the learner must output a sampler whose output distribution (conditioned on the training data) is close in total variation to the uniform distribution over $f^{-1}(1)$. Their work implicitly gives an efficient algorithm for PAC learning to sample $C$, given three primitives for $C$: an online learner, approximate sampling and counting oracles, and an SQ learner. We ask whether these ingredients, in particular online learnability, are necessary. First, we construct a Boolean concept class $C$ for which online learning is cryptographically hard, yet PAC learning to sample is computationally efficient. Then, we develop new algorithms that use offline ERM oracles instead of online learners, together with approximate sampling/counting oracles for intersections of concepts in $C$ and an SQ learner for $C$. We view our results, together with the work of De, Diakonikolas, and Servedio, as a first step towards understanding the computational complexity of language generation.
item.dc:creator: Alkis Kalavasis, Shuchen Li, Manolis Zampetakis

item.title: Node Differential Privacy via Node-Stable Graph Projections
item.description: arXiv:2611.33672v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Node-differentially private algorithms enable learning on network-structured datasets in which records reflect interactions among individuals. They protect the privacy of each individual's information, including all their associated records. A key challenge in the design of such algorithms is to exploit the structure of realistic graphs---where most nodes have low degree---to achieve high accuracy, without compromising on the worst-case privacy guarantee. In this work we give two new tools for designing accurate, computationally efficient node-differentially private algorithms. First, we give a nearly linear time, randomized, node-stable graph projection: the projection leaves graphs of maximum degree $D$ unchanged, maps arbitrary graphs to subgraphs of maximum degree $\hat D \approx D$, and ensures that changing one node of the input graph has only a small effect on the distribution of the edges selected among the remaining vertices. Unlike prior approaches, which abstain when the input violates the degree bound, our projection acts as degree clipping: even when $D$ is set well below the true maximum degree (trading truncation bias at high-degree outliers for lower privacy noise), it retains at least as many edges as a maximal $D$-bounded subgraph. Second, for graphs with bounded edge weights, we give a deterministic nearly linear time Lipschitz extension for the total edge weight that agrees with the original sum on graphs of maximum degree $D$ yet is $D$-Lipschitz on all graphs. Finally, we show how to apply these methods to design node-private algorithms for high-dimensional vector summation and gradient descent on datasets where records are associated with graph edges, such as email threads.
item.dc:creator: Ishaq Aden-Ali, Adam Sealfon, Adam Smith, Thomas Steinke, Jonathan Ullman

item.title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for TSP and More
item.description: arXiv:2611.33730v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The traveling salesman problem (TSP) is a canonical NP-hard optimization problem. For general edge weights, the classical dynamic programs of Bellman and of Held and Karp solve TSP on $n$ cities in $O^*(2^n)$ time. To date, no $\Oh(c^n)$-time classical algorithm is known for any $c<2$. Combining Grover search with the dynamic programming technique, Ambainis et al. (SODA 2019) introduced a quantum algorithm with running time $O^*(1.7274^n)$, which is still the best known quantum time bound. In this work, we improve the running time to $O^*(1.70961^n)$. The core idea of our algorithm is to combine the framework of Ambainis et al. with the extremal set-system framework, which was recently used for classical space-time tradeoffs of TSP by Jabal Ameli, Nederlof and Wang (FOCS 2026) and Dallant and Kozma (FOCS 2026). To obtain our upper bound, we decompose the optimal tour into four consecutive subpaths of different sizes, for which, based on the idea of set-systems, the optimal values are computed using dynamic programming with small success probability and use amplitude amplification. Using the same idea, we also give a new quantum space-time tradeoff for TSP, improving the previous results of Caroppo et al. (ESA 2026) and Dallant (arXiv:2607.12374). Finally, we obtain the same quantum upper bounds for several other related problems.
item.dc:creator: Masayuki Miyamoto

item.title: Tropical and maximum colorful matchings in vertex-colored graphs
item.description: arXiv:2611.34107v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A subgraph of a vertex-colored graph istropical if it contains every color. We study matchings by the number of colors they cover. A matching is maximum colorful if no matching covers more colors. When a tropical matching exists, the maximum colorful matchings are exactly the tropical matchings. We give polynomial-time algorithms for two problems: a maximum matching that covers the most colors, and a tropical matching with the fewest edges. Both algorithms rest on a counterpart of Berge's theorem: a matching is optimal if and only if it admits no tropical augmentation, or no tropical reduction. These are chains of alternating paths linked by relays, and each one is found by a single augmenting-path search in an auxiliary graph. The same tools give a maximum colorful matching with the fewest edges, and show that all maximum matchings that are maximum colorful are connected by flips. Finally, the sets of colors that a matching can cover form a matroid. The greedy algorithm then computes a matching of maximum color weight. This paper extends the conference version and the PhD thesis of one of the authors.
item.dc:creator: Johanne Cohen, Yannis Manoussakis, Hong Phong Pham, Zsolt Tuza

item.title: A Local-Counting Approach for Distributed Induced Path Detection
item.description: arXiv:2611.34185v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A well-known application of the celebrated color-coding technique is fast detection of paths in a distributed setting with limited bandwidth, by propagating a signal along colorful paths [Even et al., DISC 2017]. However, since vertices of the same color are indistinguishable by this procedure, it cannot detect induced paths, as they appear the same as cycles. We make the following observation. If, for a given edge, we \emph{count} the number of such signals over all permutations of the random coloring that terminate at that edge, then we can separate an induced path from a cycle: an induced path contributes one to that count, while a cycle contributes two. Refining and generalizing this observation gives our \emph{local-counting approach}, which allows us to separate induced paths from any other subgraph. We establish the following end results, all improving upon the state of the art in their round complexities and refined detection variants. * An $O(1)$-round algorithm for induced $P_4$ detection. * $O(\Delta)$-round algorithms for detection of induced $P_5$ and $P_6$. * An $\tilde{O}(n^{1/3})$-round algorithm for detection of induced $P_5$ in induced-$C_4$ free graphs.
item.dc:creator: Keren Censor-Hillel, Julian Ewaied

item.title: Prophet Inequalities for Mixtures of I.I.D. Random Variables
item.description: arXiv:2611.34264v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A latent index $J\in\{1,\ldots,k\}$ is drawn from a prior $\pi$. Conditional on $J=j$, a gambler observes random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ drawn independently from a non-negative component distribution $F_j$. The gambler knows $n$, the prior $\pi$, and the component distributions $F_1,\ldots,F_k$, but not $J$, observes the values sequentially, and selects at most one value at the time it is revealed. We show that the largest $\alpha$ such that the gambler can guarantee to select a value of $\alpha\cdot\mathbb{E}[\max_iX_i]$ in expectation, for all distributions where this expectation is finite, is \[ \alpha=\frac1e+\frac{1}{k^{2/3+o(1)}}. \] The lower bound is achieved by the better of two variants of the standard secretary rule. The upper bound uses a finely tuned instance of the common-scale model, which scales a sequence of independent random variables by a single latent variable.
item.dc:creator: Felix Fischer, Kevin Schewior

item.title: Square-root comparison, Turnpike, and exact semidefinite feasibility
item.description: arXiv:2611.34535v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Given positive integers $a_i,K$, put $S=\sum_{i=1}^k\sqrt{a_i}$. We construct a realizable Turnpike instance in which the minimum spacing of distinct distances and the smallest nonzero addition residual are both at most $|S-K|$ when $S\ne K$. With approximation oracles, one three-distance realizability query decides $S\le K$. For unordered lists of radical sums with nonnegative rational coefficients, a polynomial-time substitution by integers preserves every normalized ruler. We give the classical reduction of square-root comparison to exact semidefinite feasibility in both threshold directions. The comparison enters through numerical separation and marked sorting; the integer recoding needs no such comparison for unordered reconstruction.
item.dc:creator: C. S. Elder

item.title: Toward a human-friendly proof of a polynomial bound for the Directed Grid Theorem
item.description: arXiv:2611.34710v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Directed Grid Theorem of Kawarabayashi and Kreutzer [STOC 2015] states that there is a function $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that every digraph of directed treewidth at least $f(k)$ contains a cylindrical grid of order $k$ as a butterfly minor. Their function is not elementary, and Hatzel, Kreutzer, Garlet Milani, and Muzi [FOCS 2024] improved it to a tower of exponentials of height $22$, by a proof in three stages through paths and cycles of well-linked sets. In this paper we prove each stage with a polynomial bound, so that $f$ can be chosen to be a polynomial of degree $20\,031\,568$. As a consequence, Younger's conjecture, proved by Reed, Robertson, Seymour, and Thomas [Combinatorica, 1996], holds with a polynomial bound: for the polynomial $f$ that we construct, every digraph without $k$ pairwise disjoint cycles has a feedback vertex set of size at most $(k-1)f(k)$. In fact, beyond cycles, we obtain polynomial packing-covering bounds for every strongly connected digraph that is a butterfly minor of a cylindrical grid.
item.dc:creator: Victor Campos, Allen Ibiapina, Raul Lopes, Rodrigo Nogueira, Ignasi Sau

item.title: Low-degree hardness rules out eigenvalue tests but not eigenvector tests
item.description: arXiv:2611.34728v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study what low-degree hardness implies for spectral tests, with the Gaussian orthogonal ensemble (GOE) as the null distribution. We show that, once a fixed amount of Gaussian noise is added, it rules out every test based on eigenvalues, but not tests based on eigenvectors. For eigenvalues, if the low-degree advantage vanishes at logarithmic degree, then the joint law of the noisy eigenvalues converges to that of the GOE in total variation. For eigenvectors, we construct planted distributions with vanishing low-degree advantage whose eigenvalues follow the GOE law exactly at every noise level, yet whose noisy eigenvectors still distinguish them from the GOE. A single eigenvector can suffice. After a small amount of noise, a polynomial-time test that uses only the span of a fixed fraction of the top eigenvectors also succeeds, even when the low-degree advantage vanishes at a prescribed polylogarithmic degree. To prove the eigenvalue result, we split the noise into three increments. The first uses the low-degree assumption to establish eigenvalue rigidity. The second couples the two spectra through Dyson Brownian motion and applies homogenization to obtain a transport estimate. The third uses Gaussian smoothing to convert this estimate into closeness in total variation.
item.dc:creator: Xuan Chen, Shuangping Li

item.title: Monotone Crossing Lattices for Exact Binary Optimization Encodings on Rydberg Arrays
item.description: arXiv:2611.34792v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Programmable Rydberg-atom arrays realize maximum-weight independent set encoding on unit-disk graphs under the ideal blockade model, but embedding nonlocal interactions requires auxiliary atoms and limits the size of tractable instances. We introduce a four-state unit-disk crossing cell that couples directly to adjacent cells, with interfaces enforcing one-sided propagation: along occupied paths directed away from the diagonal, copy bits are nondecreasing. For the maximum-weight independent set problem, uniform cell weights guarantee that every ground state of the encoded instance decodes to an optimal solution of the original problem, even when local copies disagree. For binary quadratic objectives subject to pairwise Boolean constraints, every feasible optimum yields consistent active copies and a target weight given by an explicit constant offset minus the source objective. A rectangular variant of the architecture further encodes minimum set cover problem. Prior to constraint-induced site deletions, the full layout requires $2n^2 - n$ sites, halving the leading-order site count of a fixed complete-grid reference, while activity pruning yields an exact site count set by the propagation span. Across 18 paired benchmarks with independent ordering from a shared candidate pool, the layout reduces site counts by 12.1%-54.0%.
item.dc:creator: Liyin Hu, Shengminjie Chen, Ran Miao, Zhiyi Huang, Xiaohan Shan, Jialin Zhang, Xiaoming Sun

item.title: Dynamic Tensor Product Regression
item.description: arXiv:2210.03961v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, we initiate the study of Dynamic Tensor Product Regression. One has matrices $A_1\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\times d_1},\ldots,A_q\in \mathbb{R}^{n_q\times d_q}$ and a label vector $b\in \mathbb{R}^{n_1\ldots n_q}$, and the goal is to solve the regression problem with the design matrix $A$ being the tensor product of the matrices $A_1, A_2, \dots, A_q$ i.e. $\min_{x\in \mathbb{R}^{d_1\ldots d_q}} \|(A_1\otimes \ldots\otimes A_q)x-b\|_2$. At each time step, one matrix $A_i$ receives a sparse change, and the goal is to maintain a sketch of the tensor product $A_1\otimes\ldots \otimes A_q$ so that the regression solution can be updated quickly. Recomputing the solution from scratch for each round is very slow and so it is important to develop algorithms which can quickly update the solution with the new design matrix. Our main result is a dynamic tree data structure where any update to a single matrix can be propagated quickly throughout the tree. We show that our data structure can be used to solve dynamic versions of not only Tensor Product Regression, but also Tensor Product Spline regression (which is a generalization of ridge regression) and for maintaining Low Rank Approximations for the tensor product.
item.dc:creator: Aravind Reddy, Zhao Song, Lichen Zhang

item.title: Space Complexity Dichotomies for Subgraph Finding Problems in the Streaming Model
item.description: arXiv:2602.08002v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study the space complexity of four variants of the standard subgraph finding problem in the streaming model. Specifically, given an $n$-vertex input graph and a fixed pattern graph on at least three vertices, we consider two settings: undirected simple graphs, denoted by $G$ and $H$, and oriented graphs, denoted by $\vec{G}$ and $\vec{H}$. Depending on the setting, the task is to decide whether $G$ contains $H$ as a subgraph or as an induced subgraph, or whether $\vec{G}$ contains $\vec{H}$ as a subgraph or as an induced subgraph. Let $\textsc{Sub}(H)$, $\textsc{IndSub}(H)$, $\textsc{Sub}(\vec{H})$, and $\textsc{IndSub}(\vec{H})$ denote these four variants, respectively. An oriented graph is well-oriented if it admits a bipartition in which every arc is oriented from the same part to the other, and a vertex is internal if both its in-degree and out-degree are non-zero. For each variant, we obtain a complete dichotomy theorem, briefly summarized as follows. \begin{itemize} \item $\textsc{Sub}(H)$ can be solved by an $\tilde{O}(1)$-pass $n^{2-\Omega(1)}$-space algorithm if and only if $H$ is bipartite. \item $\textsc{IndSub}(H)$ can be solved by an $\tilde{O}(1)$-pass $n^{2-\Omega(1)}$-space algorithm if and only if $H$ is $P_3$, $P_4$, or $\mbox{co-}P_3$. \item $\textsc{Sub}(\vec{H})$ can be solved by a deterministic single-pass $n^{2-\Omega(1)}$-space algorithm if and only if every connected component of $\vec H$ is either a well-oriented bipartite graph or a tree containing at most one internal vertex. \item $\textsc{IndSub}(\vec{H})$ can be solved by an $\tilde{O}(1)$-pass $n^{2-\Omega(1)}$-space algorithm if and only if the underlying undirected simple graph $H$ is a $\mbox{co-}P_3$. \end{itemize} All our upper bounds are attained by deterministic algorithms that find a copy, whereas all our lower bounds hold even for randomized algorithms that only detect one.S
item.dc:creator: Yu-Sheng Shih, Meng-Tsung Tsai, Yen-Chu Tsai, Ying-Sian Wu

item.title: On the Assadi Liu Tarjan Auction Algorithm for Bipartite Matching: Simplification, Alternative Analysis, and Hard Instance
item.description: arXiv:2607.07439v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Assadi, Liu, and Tarjan [SOSA'21] gave an auction algorithm that outputs a $(1-\epsilon)$-approximation to Maximum Matching in bipartite graphs. Their algorithm computes a sequence of $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2})$ maximal matchings in subgraphs of the input graph and can be implemented in the multi-pass streaming setting with $O(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2})$ passes in a straightforward manner, which constitutes the state-of-the-art pass/approximation trade-off result in the multi-pass streaming setting. Their analysis uses tools from combinatorial auctions and, at its heart, relies on a clever potential function argument. Their proof, however, provides only limited insight into the inner workings of the algorithm. In this paper, we revisit the ALT-algorithm and present the following contributions. Simplification: The ALT-algorithm is built upon a freezing mechanism where vertices on one side of the bipartition that have already been rematched $\Theta(\frac{1}{\epsilon})$ times over the course of the algorithm remain matched to their current partner forever. We show that this mechanism is in fact unnecessary, i.e., no special treatment of such vertices is needed. Alternative Analysis: We give an alternative analysis of the algorithm that is based on augmenting paths. Our analysis allows for a reinterpretation as one that follows the traditional approach of searching for and eliminating augmenting paths. Our analysis also copes with the removal of the freezing mechanism in a natural way, whereas the analysis of Assadi et al. strictly depends on its use. Hard Instance: We provide the first hard instance on which the algorithm requires $\Omega(\frac{1}{\epsilon^2})$ iterations/maximal matching computations. The instance is a simple path graph, where we exhibit a cyclic behaviour that prevents fast progress.
item.dc:creator: Christian Konrad, Kheeran K. Naidu, Archie Walton, Yiquan Wang

item.title: Undirected Multiple-Unicast Network Coding and Faster External-Memory Integer Sorting
item.description: arXiv:2610.20079v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In undirected multiple-unicast networks, where independent messages are sent between specified source-destination pairs, network coding allows intermediate nodes to combine messages, whereas fractional routing splits and forwards individual messages along paths without mixing them. Proposed in 2004 by Li and Li and independently by Harvey, Kleinberg, and Lehman, the multiple-unicast conjecture---long a central open problem in network coding with deep connections to computational complexity---asserts that network coding and fractional routing have the same achievable rate region. We construct a counterexample refuting this conjecture and use it to reduce block transfers in external-memory data rearrangement, thereby accelerating external-memory integer sorting and answering in the affirmative the longstanding question of Aggarwal and Vitter (1988) on whether integer operations can beat the comparison-sorting input/output (I/O) bound. Specifically, we give a deterministic sorting algorithm: for $N$ integers of $\Theta(\log N)$ bits, a memory holding $M$ integers, and block transfers of $B$ integers, where $2B\le M\le N$, the number of block transfers is $$O\!\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{\log N}{(\log(M/B))^{1-\varepsilon}(\log M)^\varepsilon}\right]\right),$$ where $\varepsilon=1.5\times10^{-5}$ is an absolute constant. This bound asymptotically improves on the classical $\Theta\!\left(\frac{N}{B}\left[1+\frac{\log(N/M)}{\log(M/B)}\right]\right)$ comparison-sorting bound in certain parameter regimes. Under the external-memory model specified in this paper, we have formally verified the algorithm's correctness and I/O complexity bound in Lean 4. Our reduction is independent of the address-field interchange construction. Using the one from recent work on multitape integer multiplication gives the bound for every fixed $0<\varepsilon<1/2$, with an $\varepsilon$-dependent constant.
item.dc:creator: Baochun Li, Zongpeng Li, Sirui Liu

item.title: Trusted Advice for Scheduling on Unrelated Machines
item.description: arXiv:2611.29883v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Scheduling on unrelated parallel machines under standard objectives, such as makespan minimization or max-min fairness, has posed fundamental theoretical challenges for decades. A prominent example is the longstanding factor 2 approximation barrier for the Min Makespan problem established by Lenstra, Shmoys, and Tardos (1990). We investigate these fundamental challenges within the framework of algorithms with trusted advice. We consider a setting in which a trusted oracle is accessed once and reveals partial but entirely accurate structural information about an optimal solution. This framework allows us to quantify the improvements in approximation guarantees enabled by various trusted advice. We formalize a hierarchy of trusted advice oracles, ranging from a strong oracle that reveals the exact assignments of long jobs to a weaker oracle that indicates only which machines process such jobs. By exploiting this information, we obtain approximation guarantees beyond the classical worst-case barriers. In particular, we show that even the weakest oracle improves the approximation ratio for Min Makespan to $\sqrt{3}\approx 1.732$. We also obtain improved ratios of $(\sqrt{33}+1)/4\approx 1.686$ and $(5\sqrt{7})/8 \approx 1.654$ for Restricted Assignment and Graph Balancing, respectively. For the max-min fairness objective, known as the Santa Claus problem, we obtain a 2-approximation using our weak oracle. Finally, we show that these problems remain NP-hard to approximate within certain constant factors even with the trusted advice oracles considered. Interestingly, for the Santa Claus problem, we show a lower bound of 2 which is tight and matches the classical oracle-free bound.
item.dc:creator: Baruch Schieber, Hadas Shachnai, Tami Tamir

item.title: Testing Expansion without Connectivity via Return Probabilities
item.description: arXiv:2611.32677v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study whether every connected component of a bounded-degree graph is an edge expander, given access to its neighbor lists. Dinur and Goldreich give a tester using $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)n^\alpha$ queries for every fixed $\alpha>2/3$. We obtain \[ \widetilde O_{d,c,\beta}\!\left(\frac{n^{1/2+\beta}}{\varepsilon} +\frac{\sqrt n}{\varepsilon^4}\right) \] queries for every fixed $0<\beta\le1$. The tester accepts graphs whose components have edge expansion at least $c$ and rejects graphs $\varepsilon$-far from having edge expansion at least $\kappa\beta c^2/d$ in every component (for an absolute constant $\kappa>0$), each with probability at least $2/3$. No structural promise is imposed on the input. The tester compares pairwise collision probabilities at two walk lengths and starts further walks at vertices where sampled endpoints coincide. These additional samples control the contribution of vertices with larger return probabilities. We show that the resulting conditions force the longer walk to be nearly uniform on an induced expander with few edges leaving it. For fixed degree $d\ge3$ and completeness threshold $0<c<(d-2\sqrt{d-1})/2$, we show that a sufficiently small rejection expansion threshold of $\gamma d$ requires $n^{1/2+\Omega_d(\gamma)}$ queries when $\varepsilon$ is a sufficiently small multiple of $\gamma$. Thus the dependence of the excess query exponent on the rejection threshold is optimal up to constant factors in this regime. We also prove an $\Omega(\sqrt{n/\log n})$ lower bound for Cayley graphs at infinitely many input sizes.
item.dc:creator: Nikolas Melissaris

item.title: Parameterized Complexity of Finding a Maximum Common Vertex Subgraph Without Isolated Vertices
item.description: arXiv:2602.10948v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: In this paper, we study the Maximum Common Vertex Subgraph problem: Given two input graphs $G_1,G_2$ and a non-negative integer $h$, is there a common subgraph $H$ on at least $h$ vertices such that there is no isolated vertex in $H$. In other words, each connected component of $H$ has at least $2$ vertices. This problem naturally arises in graph theory along with other variants of the well-studied Maximum Common Subgraph problem and also has applications in computational social choice. We show that this problem is NP-hard and provide an FPT algorithm when parameterized by $h$. Next, we conduct a study of the problem on common structural parameters like vertex cover number, maximum degree, treedepth, pathwidth and treewidth of one or both input graphs. We derive a complete dichotomy of parameterized results for our problem with respect to individual parameterizations as well as combinations of parameterizations from the above structural parameters. This provides us with a deep insight into the complexity theoretic and parameterized landscape of this problem.
item.dc:creator: Palash Dey, Anubhav Dhar, Ashlesha Hota, Sudeshna Kolay, Aritra Mitra

item.title: On the Parameterized Complexity of Coloring Discovery
item.description: arXiv:2609.09837v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Coloring Discovery asks whether a possibly improper initial coloring can be made proper within a prescribed number of allowed changes. We study the parameterized complexity of three modification step models that were studied previously in the literature: recoloring one vertex (color flipping), swapping the colors of arbitrary vertices (color swapping), and swapping colors only across an edge (color sliding). For color flipping, we give exact fixed-parameter algorithms for the parameters vertex cover and distance to complete. For color swapping, we obtain fixed-parameter tractability for the parameter vertex cover plus the number of colors. Our lower bounds show W[1]-hardness for treedepth plus feedback vertex set in the color flipping model and for the number of colors plus bandwidth or distance to disjoint paths in the swapping and sliding models. All three variants remain NP-complete with four colors on graphs of diameter two.
item.dc:creator: Eric Decker, Sebastian Siebertz

item.title: Policy Iteration Is Not Polynomial for Deterministic Markov Decision Processes: The Price of Algorithmic Anarchy
item.description: arXiv:2609.40147v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We establish exponential iteration lower bounds in the number of states for Howard's policy iteration on deterministic discounted and average-reward Markov decision processes (MDPs), with a constant number of actions per state. This rules out polynomial-time complexity of Howard's policy iteration in both settings. We further prove that a Dantzig counterpart of Howard's policy iteration runs in strongly polynomial time on deterministic average-reward MDPs. Together with the known strongly polynomial bound for Dantzig's rule on deterministic discounted MDPs, these results establish an exponential separation between the two algorithms in both settings. This separation between Howard's decentralized and simultaneous selfish improvements and Dantzig's coordinated selection of a single action with the largest improvement across all states reveals a "price" of algorithmic anarchy.
item.dc:creator: Han Zhong, Yinyu Ye

item.title: Computing EF1 Allocations under Budget Constraints in Polynomial Time
item.description: arXiv:2611.12740v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study the allocation of indivisible goods to agents with budgets and additive valuations. Each agent compares its bundle with every budget-feasible subset of another agent's bundle or of the unallocated goods. We give a strongly polynomial algorithm for computing an allocation that is envy-free up to one good (EF1), even when agents have different valuations and budgets. Deciding whether a given allocation satisfies EF1 is coNP-complete. Equivalently, deciding whether it violates EF1 is NP-complete. When all agents have the same valuation, we can compute an EF1 allocation with welfare at least $(1/2-\varepsilon)$ times the maximum feasible welfare in time polynomial in the input length and $1/\varepsilon$, for any $0<\varepsilon<1/2$. Finding an allocation that is envy-free up to any good (EFX) is NP-hard even for one agent. We give polynomial-time EFX algorithms when each agent values goods in proportion to their sizes or when the number of distinct positive item values per agent is bounded by a constant.
item.dc:creator: Tingwei Hu, Lili Mei, Guochuan Zhang
